readerTitle: How a web design shop paid for a $12 billion company
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Mailchimp, Intuit 인수) + 가상 적용 (주택 도장 업체의 견적 앱)
insight: 기존 서비스 사업의 현금이 새 사업의 첫 투자자가 될 수 있다. 그 대가로 속도를 내주고 소유권을 지킨다.
misconception: 큰 회사를 만들려면 반드시 외부 투자를 받아야 하고, 투자 없이 자란 회사는 작게 남는다.

sources.text: Intuit press release, 'Intuit to Acquire Mailchimp' (September 13, 2021): 약 120억 달러 현금·주식 인수
Mailchimp 공식 회사 소개 'Our Story' (2001년 Rocket Science Group의 부업으로 시작, 외부 투자 없음)
Ben Chestnut 인터뷰 및 언론 보도 (2007년 에이전시 정리, 2009년 무료 요금제 도입)
2021년 인수 후 직원 보상 관련 언론 보도 (직원 지분 부재에 대한 비판)

factChecks.note: 인수 금액 약 120억 달러(현금+주식), 발표일 2021년 9월 13일은 Intuit 보도자료로 확인하세요. 인수 완료는 2021년 11월로 알려져 있습니다.
창업자(Ben Chestnut, Dan Kurzius)가 회사를 사실상 전부 소유했다는 내용은 여러 언론 보도에 기반합니다. 정확한 지분율은 공개 자료로 확인되지 않아 카드에는 'nearly all'로만 적었습니다.
에이전시를 정리하고 Mailchimp에 집중한 시점(2007년경)과 무료 요금제 도입(2009년)은 창업자 인터뷰 기준입니다. 무료 요금제 이후 가입자 증가폭 수치는 자료마다 달라 카드에는 수치를 넣지 않았습니다.
Mailchimp의 매출 규모는 수치 대신 정성적으로만 표현했습니다. 인수 직원 보상 비판도 구체 금액 없이 일반적으로 서술했습니다. 게시 전 보도 내용을 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: How a web design shop paid for a $12 billion company
body: In 2021, Intuit agreed to buy Mailchimp, the email marketing company, for about $12 billion in cash and stock.

Mailchimp had never taken money from venture investors. It started in 2001 as a side project inside a small Atlanta web design agency. The agency's client work paid the bills while the side project grew.

image.label: A small design studio with a tiny email product growing out of it
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 디자인 사무실 책상 위 모니터에서 편지 봉투 모양 식물이 자라나 사무실보다 커지는 장면. 실제 Mailchimp 로고나 원숭이 캐릭터는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The side project is starting to work.
body: It's the mid-2000s. You co-run a web design agency. Client projects pay steadily, but the work is tiring. Your email tool for small businesses is growing on its own, with customers paying monthly.

options.text: Raise venture money, quit client work and grow the tool fast
options.feedback: You gain speed and a bigger team right away. You give up a share of ownership and agree to grow on investors' timeline.

options.text: Keep the agency as the main business and the tool as a side line
options.feedback: It's the safest path for your income. But the tool only gets your leftover hours, and a focused rival may pass you.

options.text: Close the agency once the tool's revenue can carry you, and grow from customer payments
options.feedback: You keep ownership and control. Growth is limited to what customers pay, and you lose the agency's steady cash.

choice.afterReveal: Mailchimp's founders chose C: they wound down the agency around 2007 and never raised outside capital.

cards.title: The agency was the first investor.
body: For years, client work covered salaries and rent. The email tool didn't need outside money because the agency funded its slow start.

Once Mailchimp's subscriptions could pay the team, the founders stepped away from client work. In 2009 they added a **free plan**. Sign-ups grew sharply, and enough free users later upgraded to paid plans to keep funding growth.
Each stage was paid for by the stage before it.

image.label: Three steps: agency cash, paid subscriptions, free plan
image.brief: 계단 세 칸 인포그래픽. 1단 "Agency client work", 2단 "Paid subscriptions", 3단 "Free plan → upgrades". 각 계단에서 동전이 다음 계단으로 굴러 올라감. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Bootstrapping
body: **Bootstrapping** means funding a business from its own revenue, or from another business you already run, instead of from investors.
Mailchimp shows a pattern many owners miss: a steady service business can act as the investor for a new product. It gives you cash and time, and it asks for no shares in return.

cards.title: What bootstrapping kept, and what it cost.
body: Because no investors held shares, the founders reportedly owned nearly all of the company when it sold. There was no **dilution**, the shrinking of your share when new owners buy in.

breakdown.label: Ownership at sale
breakdown.detail: No investor shares to pay out

breakdown.label: Control
breakdown.detail: No board pushing for a fast exit

breakdown.label: Time to sale
breakdown.detail: Growth limited by what customers paid

breakdown.label: Risk
breakdown.detail: No outside cushion if things went wrong

cards.title: The conditions mattered as much as the choice.
list: **Cheap to serve one more customer:** software costs little per extra user
**Monthly payments:** cash came in before costs piled up
**Overlooked customers:** small businesses that bigger rivals ignored
**Patience:** the founders could wait two decades
cards.callout: Remove these conditions and the same choice could have meant being outrun.

cards.title: One success story isn't a rule.
body: We hear about Mailchimp because it won. Many bootstrapped companies stay small or get outspent by funded rivals in markets where speed decides the winner.

Ownership also cuts both ways. After the sale, Mailchimp faced public criticism because most employees held no shares and didn't share directly in the $12 billion. If you bootstrap, decide early how the people who build it will share in the upside.

cards.title: Now it's a house-painting company.
body: You run a painting crew with steady demand. You built a phone app to price jobs from photos, and three other painting firms now want to pay for it monthly.
How do you fund the app?

options.text: Keep the crew running, charge the firms monthly, and hire for the app only as its revenue grows
options.feedback: Your painting income buys you time, and paying customers prove demand. Growth is slower, but you keep the business and the risk stays small.

options.text: Sell the crew and raise investor money to grow the app nationwide
options.feedback: It could move fast, but three customers is thin proof for giving up both your income and a share of ownership.

options.text: Give the app away free to get big fast, paid for with credit cards
options.feedback: Free can grow use, but with no revenue and expensive debt, your cash runs out before you learn if anyone will pay.

cards.title: Your current business can be your first investor.
body: Bootstrapping trades speed for ownership and control. It works best when each sale costs little to serve, customers pay early, and you can afford to be patient.
**Try it today:** list what your current business could fund for the next 12 months. What new line could grow on that cash without outside money?
